cards.title: What happens when you run out?
cards.body:
[[IPv4]] has about 4.3 billion addresses, and there are more connected devices than that. The organisations that hand out addresses gave away their last big blocks of IPv4 addresses in the 2010s.

Sharing addresses with [[NAT]] helps a lot, but it's a workaround. The real fix is a new version of the Internet [[Protocol]] with far longer addresses: **IPv6**, which is version 6.

options.text: IPv4 didn't have enough addresses for every device
IPv4 was too slow for video
options.nudge: IPv6 isn't about speed. Think about the problem that NAT was used to work around.

options.text: To replace website names like example.com
options.nudge: Names like example.com are still used. IPv6 is a new kind of address, so what was wrong with the old kind?

options.text: To make addresses shorter and easier to remember
options.nudge: IPv6 addresses are far longer than IPv4 ones, so being easy to remember can't be the reason. What did IPv4 have a problem with?

cards.explanation: IPv6 exists because IPv4's 32-bit addresses **ran out**. It doesn't replace names like `example.com`, and it isn't about speed. And as you're about to see, IPv6 addresses are much *longer* than IPv4 ones, not easier to remember.
cards.hint: Think about the problem that [[NAT]] was a workaround for.

cards.title: 128 bits, written in hex
cards.body:
An [[IPv6]] address is **128 [[bits|bit]]** long, four times the length of an [[IPv4]] address. That gives about 340 trillion trillion trillion addresses, enough to never run out.

Writing 128 bits in [[binary]] would be far too long, so IPv6 uses **hex**, from the last module. Remember: each hex digit stands for 4 bits. An IPv6 address is written as **8 groups** of **4 hex digits**, separated by colons:

`2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001`

Addresses starting `2001:db8` are reserved for examples, like `192.0.2.x` in IPv4.

cards.prompt: Each group in an [[IPv6]] address has 4 [[hex]] digits. How many **bits** is one group?
cards.hint: Each hex digit stands for 4 bits.
cards.explanation: Each hex digit is 4 bits, so 4 digits make 4 × 4 = **16 bits**. And 8 groups of 16 bits make 8 × 16 = 128 bits, the whole address.
cards.nudge: A group has 4 hex digits, and each hex digit stands for 4 bits. Multiply those together.

cards.title: Two rules for shortening
cards.body:
[[IPv6]] addresses often contain lots of zeros, so there are two rules for writing them shorter.

**Rule 1:** drop the zeros at the *start* of any group. `0db8` becomes `db8`, `0000` becomes `0`, and `0001` becomes `1`. Zeros at the end of a group stay, so `ff00` stays `ff00`.

**Rule 2:** replace one row of all-zero groups that sit side by side with a double colon, `::`. You can only do this **once** in an address.

`2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001`

becomes `2001:db8:0:0:0:0:0:1` after rule 1, and `2001:db8::1` after rule 2.

cards.prompt: What is the shortest correct way to write `2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329`?

options.nudge: Rule 1 only removes zeros at the **start** of a group. Check what happened to zeros at the end of a group here.
Count the groups. If zero groups vanish without `::`, nothing shows where they were. Rule 2 needs that marker.
Only zeros at the start of a group can go. Zeros in the middle of a group have to stay.

cards.explanation:
Drop leading zeros (`0db8` → `db8`, `0042` → `42`), then replace the three zero groups with `::` to get `2001:db8::ff00:42:8329`.

- `ff00` can't become `ff`: only zeros at the **start** of a group can go.
- Without `::`, there are only 5 groups and nothing shows where the missing zeros were.
- `2001` can't become `21`: those zeros are in the middle, not at the start.
cards.hint: Apply rule 1 to every group first (only zeros at the start go), then rule 2 to the run of all-zero groups.

cards.prompt: Match each value to what it is.
cards.explanation: IPv4 uses four decimal numbers with **dots**. IPv6 uses hex groups with **colons**. `example.com` is a name for people, not an address. `11000000` is 192 in binary, and `C8` is 200 in hex.
cards.hint: Look closely at each value: is it split by dots or colons, and which digits or letters does it use?
cards.nudge: IPv4 is four decimal numbers separated by dots, and IPv6 is hex groups separated by colons. The rest here aren't addresses.

cards.prompt: Why can `::` only appear **once** in an [[IPv6]] address?

options.text: With two, you couldn't tell how many zero groups each one stands for
Because :: is only allowed at the very end of an address
options.nudge: `::` isn't limited to the end: in `2001:db8::1` it sits in the middle. Think about what a reader needs to rebuild all 8 groups.

options.text: Because the address would become shorter than 128 bits
options.nudge: However it's written, an IPv6 address is still 128 bits underneath. Think about how a reader would know where the zeros go.

options.text: There's no real reason, it's just tradition
options.nudge: There is a real reason. Try writing an address with `::` in two places, then turning it back into the full 8 groups.

cards.explanation: Take `2001:db8::1::1`. It has 4 groups written out, so 4 zero groups are missing, but how are they split? It could mean `2001:db8:0:1:0:0:0:1` or `2001:db8:0:0:0:1:0:1`, and more. With only one `::`, there's only one place the missing groups can go. `::` can appear at the start, middle or end, and the address is always 128 bits underneath.
cards.hint: A full address always has 8 groups. If `::` hides some of them, what does a reader need to know to put them back?

cards.prompt: [[IPv6]] has 2¹²⁸ addresses and [[IPv4]] has 2³². IPv6 has **2 to the power of what** times as many?
cards.hint: 2¹²⁸ is 2 multiplied by itself 128 times. How many of those 2s are left if you cancel out 32 of them?
cards.explanation: Dividing 2¹²⁸ by 2³² cancels out 32 of the 128 twos, leaving 128 − 32 = **96**. So IPv6 has 2⁹⁶ times as many addresses as IPv4: roughly 79 thousand trillion trillion times as many.
cards.nudge: Dividing cancels some of the 2s. You don't need the huge numbers, only the power: how many 2s are left over?

cards.prompt: Most devices today have **both** an [[IPv4]] and an [[IPv6]] address. This laptop runs [[Linux]]. Run `ip -brief addr` and find the IPv6 address that starts with `2001:db8`. Each line is one connection: `wlan0` is the Wi-Fi, and `lo` is the laptop talking to itself.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Show this computer's addresses, one line per connection
Show this computer's addresses in full detail
commands.output:
1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 65536 qdisc noqueue state UNKNOWN group default qlen 1000
    link/loopback 00:00:00:00:00:00 brd 00:00:00:00:00:00
    inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
    inet6 ::1/128 scope host
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
2: wlan0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc noqueue state UP group default qlen 1000
    link/ether 00:00:5e:00:53:01 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    inet 192.168.1.42/24 brd 192.168.1.255 scope global dynamic wlan0
       valid_lft 86143sec preferred_lft 86143sec
    inet6 2001:db8:1:2::42/64 scope global dynamic mngtmpaddr
       valid_lft 86251sec preferred_lft 14251sec
    inet6 fe80::1/64 scope link
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever

success.question: What is the laptop's 2001:db8 IPv6 address? (Leave off the /64 at the end.)

cards.explanation:
The `wlan0` line (the Wi-Fi connection) lists `2001:db8:1:2::42`. The `/64` after it describes the size of the [[network]], which isn't part of the address itself.

The same line also shows the IPv4 address `192.168.1.42`, so this laptop uses both versions at once. `::1` and `127.0.0.1` are special addresses a computer uses to talk to itself, and `fe80::1` only works on the local network.
cards.hint: Run `ip -brief addr`, then look along the `wlan0` line for the address that begins with `2001:db8`.
cards.nudge: Copy the address exactly as shown, starting at `2001:db8` and stopping before the `/`. The other addresses on that line are different ones.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- [[IPv4]] ran out of addresses, so **IPv6** was created.
- An IPv6 address is **128 [[bits|bit]]**, written as 8 groups of 4 [[hex]] digits separated by colons.
- To shorten one: drop zeros at the **start** of each group, and replace **one** run of all-zero groups with `::`.
- Most devices use IPv4 and IPv6 side by side.

That's the end of the lessons in this module. Take the quiz to unlock the next one: how data actually travels across the internet.
